title: Fed's Internal Divide on Rate Hikes Deepens as Five Years of High Inflation Tests Patience
excerpt: Three FOMC members dissented in favor of raising rates at the July meeting, the widest split under Chairman Warsh, as 30-year Treasury yields hit a 19-year high on inflation fears.
body:
• The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate steady at 3.5-3.75% in a 9-3 vote on July 29, with three FOMC members dissenting in favor of a quarter-point rate hike — the widest split since Chairman Kevin Warsh took the helm in May.
  • Warsh declared there is "no soft inflation target" at the Fed, reinforcing his commitment to the 2% goal after five years of elevated prices, but stopped short of backing an immediate increase.
  • The decision triggered a sharp selloff in long-term Treasuries, pushing the 30-year yield to a 19-year high of 5.24%, which markets interpreted as a vote of no confidence in the Fed's inaction.
  • Futures markets are now pricing a 67% probability of a rate hike at the September meeting, up sharply from pre-meeting levels.

The Federal Reserve's internal divisions over monetary policy have reached their most visible point in years, with three FOMC members voting to raise interest rates at the July 29 meeting while Chairman Kevin Warsh held the line on keeping rates unchanged. The 9-3 split — the widest dissent under Warsh's leadership — laid bare the growing tension between officials who want to move preemptively against inflation and those who believe patience is still warranted.

The Decision and the Dissent

The Federal Open Market Committee voted to leave the federal funds rate in a range of 3.5% to 3.75%, the fifth consecutive hold. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, Cleveland's Beth Hammack, and Minneapolis Fed Chief Neel Kashkari dissented, each preferring a quarter-percentage-point increase, according to the post-meeting statement.

The committee's statement was nearly identical to its June counterpart, reiterating that "inflation remains elevated relative to the Committee's 2 percent goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy." Officials repeated their pledge to "deliver price stability."

But the real fireworks came during Warsh's press conference.

"For some households, businesses and market professionals, five years of high inflation have left a mistaken impression — that's hard to shake — that the Fed's implicit inflation target was somehow above 2%. Let me reiterate: There is no soft inflation target. There is no soft implicit target, not on this committee's watch."

— Kevin Warsh, Federal Reserve Chairman

Markets Respond With a Split Verdict

The bond market delivered its own judgment. Long-term Treasury yields surged, with the 30-year yield climbing above 5.2% — a 19-year high — in what analysts described as a vote of no confidence in the Fed's ability to bring inflation down without raising rates. The selloff deepened after Warsh appeared to hint that the central bank might reconsider its 2% inflation target framework, though he later clarified his commitment to the existing goal.

Short-term yields moved in the opposite direction. The two-year Treasury yield fell from 4.34% to 4.24% as markets pared back expectations of how far the Fed might ultimately raise rates. Fed funds futures priced in a roughly 60% chance of a quarter-point hike at the September 16 meeting, rising to over 70% by October and above 80% by December, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.

Deeper Divisions Beneath the Surface

The three formal dissents understate the breadth of hawkish sentiment within the FOMC. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem, who is not a voting member this year, told the Financial Times he had "expressed a preference" for a rate increase at the meeting. Minutes from the June meeting, released in July, showed officials "deeply divided" — with "many" expecting rates to be unchanged or lower by year-end, but "many" also anticipating they would need to be higher.

Nine of the 19 FOMC participants now project at least one rate hike by the end of 2026, according to the Fed's most recent quarterly projections. Warsh abstained from submitting his own projection.

"At this juncture, earlier, incremental, gradual interest-rate action is preferable, less costly and less disruptive than potentially later, larger and abrupt actions," Musalem told the FT, warning that the Treasury selloff signaled the Fed needed to earn its inflation-fighting "credibility" with action, not just rhetoric.

What Is Driving the Debate

Inflation has been running above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years. A spike in gasoline prices driven by the U.S.-Iran conflict pushed the annual rate to 4.2% in May, its highest level in over three years. While oil and gas prices moderated somewhat in June — producing the first monthly decline in consumer prices in six years — renewed fighting around the Strait of Hormuz has reignited concerns that pump prices could stay elevated.

Adding to the complexity, the massive capital expenditure cycle driven by artificial intelligence is putting upward pressure on prices for semiconductors, electricity, and building materials. Many Fed officials worry that AI-driven demand could keep inflation elevated even if energy prices ease, according to the June meeting minutes.

Warsh acknowledged this tension but signaled that market forces were doing some of the tightening work. "Markets have made decisions because we step back in part from trying to influence those," he said, noting that Treasury yields had moved higher on their own. "Market judgments have moved up on what nominal rates are across the Treasury curve."

What to Watch Next

The September FOMC meeting is shaping up as the most consequential policy decision of Warsh's young chairmanship. A Reuters poll found that over three-quarters of economists expect rates to remain unchanged through year-end, but financial markets disagree — futures pricing reflects a two-thirds probability of a hike in September alone. If August inflation data comes in hot, the pressure on Warsh to join the hawkish camp will intensify. For now, the chairman appears to be walking a narrow line: talking tough on inflation while hoping that market-driven tightening and easing energy prices will do the job without a politically charged rate increase.
